label: Work and Life Balance
framing: Work is a good thing that becomes a hard master the moment it stops being one part of life and starts being all of it. Scripture frames work as worship and rest as command, and it builds into the very rhythm of the week a hard stop, a day that says you are not what you produce.
cultural: Our economy rewards the always-on and treats rest as a luxury or a weakness, so we answer the message at midnight and bring the laptop on vacation and wear our exhaustion like a badge. We have let work colonize the family table and the Lord's day both, then wonder why we feel hollow. Many of us have given our best hours to the job and the leftovers to the people we love, and called ourselves providers.
historical: The Sabbath was radical when it was given, a weekly day off commanded for slave and free and animal alike in a world that knew no such mercy, thirty-three centuries before any labor law. The Reformers recovered ordinary work as a calling, but they kept the rhythm, knowing work without rest is not devotion but pride. Eugene Peterson and others in our own time have named burnout as a spiritual failure to keep the Sabbath God built into us.
application: Build a real boundary and defend it, a time when work is done and the phone is down and the people in front of you have your face. Keep a weekly Sabbath, a full day to rest and worship and remember you are not indispensable. Do your work as unto the Lord while you are in it, and then leave it, trusting that the One who feeds the birds will feed you too. The harder you find it to stop, the more you need to.

verses.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain. In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat— for He gives sleep to His beloved.
verses.where: A song of ascents says that building, guarding and working from early to late are in vain unless the LORD builds and guards, for he gives sleep to those he loves. The site's plain note says the psalm does not tell anyone to stop working, since builders still build and watchmen still watch; it says that worry is not the same as work. Lying down to rest can be an act of trust that God keeps the city while you sleep.

verses.text: Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways! For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours. Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house, your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table.
verses.where: The twin of Psalm 127 pictures the happiness of those who fear the LORD as a household: eating the fruit of one's own labor, and a table with people around it. The site's plain note calls it a picture of ordinary life made good and says it ends as a prayer, treating these things as gifts and not wages; a home without a spouse or children is not less blessed in God's eyes. Work in this psalm is for the table, not the other way round.

verses.text: Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun—all your fleeting days. For this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun. Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might, for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom.
verses.where: The Teacher has looked hard at death, and the site's note on the chapter says that because of it he urges his reader to eat, drink, love his wife and work with all his might. In this passage enjoying life with the one you love and doing your work wholeheartedly stand side by side as the portion God gives. Neither is allowed to swallow the other.

verses.text: If a man is newly married, he must not be sent to war or be pressed into any duty. For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married.
verses.where: The law exempts a newly married man from war and from any public duty for a year, so that he can stay at home and bring joy to his wife. The site's note on the chapter lists it beside the laws that protect the poor, and the note on Luke 14 recalls the same exemption. Israel's law made room in public duty for the joy of a home.

verses.text: Six days you shall labor, but on the seventh day you shall rest; even in the seasons of plowing and harvesting, you must rest.
verses.where: When the covenant is renewed, the Sabbath command returns with a new clause: rest even in the seasons of plowing and harvest. The site's note says these were the two seasons when every hour counted on a farm, and that by keeping the Sabbath then Israel confessed that its harvest depended on God and not only on its own labor. The busy season is exactly when the rest is tested.

verses.text: But Martha was distracted by all the preparations to be made. She came to Jesus and said, “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!” “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”
verses.where: Martha is distracted by all the preparations and asks Jesus to send her sister back to help, and he answers that she is worried and upset about many things, but only one thing is necessary. The site's note says Martha's hospitality was good and needed, and the plain note says the trouble was not that she served but that she served anxious and resentful. It adds that Jesus is not scolding the one who keeps everything running; he is inviting her to sit down too.

verses.text: As it was, the heat consumed me by day and the frost by night, and sleep fled from my eyes. Thus for twenty years I have served in your household—fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flocks—and you have changed my wages ten times! If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely by now you would have sent me away empty-handed. But God has seen my affliction and the toil of my hands, and last night He rendered judgment.”
verses.where: Jacob recites twenty years of service to Laban: heat by day, frost by night, sleep fleeing from his eyes, and wages changed ten times. The site's note says faithful work does not require silence about injustice, and that Jacob confesses his wealth rested on God's presence and not on his own cleverness. The plain note says God saw his affliction and the work of his hands.

verses.text: But one after another they all began to make excuses. The first one said, ‘I have bought a field, and I need to go see it. Please excuse me.’ Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.’ Still another said, ‘I have married a wife, so I cannot come.’
verses.where: In Jesus' parable the invited guests make excuses: a field to see, oxen to try out, a new marriage. The site's note says land, livestock and marriage are good gifts and none of the excuses is sinful in itself; the parable shows how good things become reasons not to come. The plain note asks which good things in your own life have become your polite excuse.

verses.text: Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil. Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred.
verses.where: Two better-than sayings set a little with the fear of the LORD above great treasure with turmoil, and a dish of vegetables with love above a fattened ox with hatred. The site's note on the chapter says they prize a little with love over plenty with turmoil. A richer table bought with an absent or angry household is a poorer one.

verses.text: Now people were bringing the little children to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them, and the disciples rebuked those who brought them. But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
verses.where: People bring little children to Jesus, the disciples rebuke them, and Jesus is indignant, the only place the Gospels use that word of him. The site's note says the scene turns the disciples' sense of who deserves Jesus' time upside down. The plain note asks who the people are in your home who seem to slow down the important work.

misread.taken: Provide for your own household is quoted to defend working every hour there is, as though long absence from home were simply obedience, and sometimes to shame a person who cannot earn enough as if they had denied the faith.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Paul is speaking of people who could care for their widowed mothers and grandmothers and would not, leaving the church to carry what they could carry themselves, and not of people who are poor, sick, out of work or unable to help. It calls the verse a call to love your own family in practical ways, and never a reason to shame someone who is struggling. Providing for a household is part of loving it, and the verse does not ask anyone to stop being present to the people it names.
misread.text: If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

whole: Most people who struggle here do not hate their families or love their work too much in any simple sense. The phone is on the table at dinner because a client might call. The laptop comes on holiday because the project cannot wait. Weekends fill with the work that did not fit the week, and the children learn which parent will be at the game. Many tell themselves it is for the family, and much of the time that is partly true. Others are not driven by ambition at all but by fear: of falling behind, of losing the job, of not having enough. The cost is usually counted late, by a spouse who has stopped asking or a child who has stopped expecting.

Scripture names the trouble without despising work. Martha's hospitality was good and needed; the site's note says the trouble was that she served anxious and resentful. The guests in Jesus' parable were not wicked; they had fields and oxen and a new marriage, good things that became reasons not to come. Psalm 127 says that rising early and staying up late, as if everything depended on us, is in vain, and the plain note says worry is not the same as work. When work takes the whole of life, it is often because something else has quietly taken God's place as the one who keeps the city: our effort, our standing, our fear of what happens if we stop.

So the Bible's wisdom is a rhythm, and it is concrete. Israel was told to rest even in plowing time and harvest, the very seasons when stopping seemed impossible. A newly married man was kept at home for a year to bring joy to his wife, and the law held public duty back to make room for it. The Teacher puts loving your spouse and doing your work with all your might side by side as one portion. Proverbs prefers a plate of vegetables with love to a feast with turmoil. In practice that means a time when work stops and is defended, people at home given your attention and not your leftovers, and honesty with an employer when the demands are unjust, as Jacob was honest with Laban. Where the job truly cannot change for a season, it means telling your family the truth about the season and its end.

The hope Scripture gives is that God gives sleep to those he loves. Jacob worked twenty years for a man who cheated him, and God saw the toil of his hands. Jesus made time for the children his disciples thought were in the way, and he did not scold Martha but invited her to sit down. The work will still be there. The people at the table will not always be, and the Lord who holds both is not asking you to carry the city on your own.
deep.sit: Who at your table has been getting your leftovers, and what would one defended evening a week look like for them?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says the psalm points to a joy that does not depend on the harvest, and suggests praying verse 8 slowly, more than once, when sleep will not come. Pray it at the end of a working day, before the phone goes down.
prayer.text: Many ask, “Who can show us the good?” Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD. You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound. I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
